title: A First-Timer's K-Drama Filming Locations Tour of Seoul: 2 Nights, 3 Days Itinerary
html:
If you've ever paused a Korean drama just to stare at the background — "wait, is that a real place?" — the answer is almost always yes. Seoul (and a few spots just outside it) is full of real cafes, parks, palaces, and department stores that show up on screen all the time. This 2-night, 3-day route is built for first-time visitors who are also K-drama fans: no car needed, everything reachable by subway or a short train ride, and no Korean required.

A quick heads-up before you start: K-dramas and K-pop videos are filmed on tight schedules, and cafes, shops, and sets change hands or close down more often than tourist attractions do. Everything below was double-checked against recent sources, but it's smart to search the location's name plus "2026" the night before you go, just to confirm it's still open and looks the way you expect.

Day 1 Morning: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP)

Start at Dongdaemun Design Plaza, the huge, curvy silver building that looks like a spaceship landed in the middle of Seoul. It was designed by the architect Zaha Hadid and opened in 2014. You don't need a drama-specific reason to visit — DDP's futuristic shape and colorful "LED Rose Garden" light installation make it one of the most-photographed backdrops in Korean dramas and K-pop music videos simply because directors love how it looks on camera.

It's directly connected to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station (subway lines 2, 4, and 5), so there's no walking required from the train. The building and surrounding park are free to walk around; only special exhibitions inside charge admission. Give yourself about an hour, more if there's an exhibition or night market running.


Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — source

Day 1 Afternoon & Evening: Myeongdong and N Seoul Tower

Walk or take a short subway ride to Myeongdong, Seoul's busiest shopping street and a stand-in for "typical Seoul" in countless dramas — the kind of crowded, neon-lit street-food scene you've probably seen a main character walk through while eating a snack on a stick. It's also just a genuinely good place to shop for cosmetics and try street food, so it earns its spot even without the drama connection.

As it gets dark, head up Namsan Mountain to N Seoul Tower, either by cable car or the free shuttle bus from Myeongdong. The tower's observation deck and its famous "locks of love" fence — where couples attach padlocks as a promise — have shown up as a romantic set piece in dramas for years, most famously in a marriage-proposal scene from the hit series My Love from the Star. Going up to the observation deck costs a separate ticket from the cable car; buying both together online ahead of time is usually cheaper than paying at the gate.


Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — source

Day 2 Morning & Midday: Yeonnam-dong and Seongsu-dong

Day 2 is about the neighborhoods that current dramas actually film in — not historic landmarks, but the cafes and side streets where "ordinary Seoul" scenes happen. Start at Yeonnam-dong, a laid-back area near Hongik University famous for the Gyeongui Line Forest Park, a long, narrow park built on an old railway line. Locals nicknamed this stretch "Yeontral Park" (a mashup of Yeonnam-dong and New York's Central Park), and its relaxed, tree-lined streets are a favorite backdrop for slice-of-life drama scenes. Grab a coffee from one of the many small cafes along the park and just walk the path — it costs nothing and takes about 30–40 minutes end to end.

From there, take the subway to Seongsu-dong, a former factory district now packed with warehouse-style cafes and boutiques — often called "Seoul's Brooklyn." One standout, Grandpa Factory (할아버지 공장), a few minutes' walk from Seongsu Station, is a converted factory cafe with a real treehouse inside that you can climb up into. It has appeared in the drama Vincenzo and several Korean variety shows. Even if you've never seen that particular drama, the space itself is worth the visit.


Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — source

Day 2 Evening: Han River Picnic at Yeouido

Almost every Korean drama eventually has a scene where two characters sit by the Han River eating fried chicken and drinking beer — and this is genuinely something Koreans do all the time, not just a TV thing. Head to Yeouido Hangang Park in the late afternoon. On the way, you'll pass The Hyundai Seoul, a glass-fronted department store that played the glamorous "Queens" department store in the hit drama Queen of Tears — worth a quick look even if you're not buying anything.

At the park, convenience stores and small delivery shops sell exactly what you need: fried chicken, beer or soju, and mats to sit on. Many locals just order delivery chicken straight to a spot on the grass using an app, then sit and watch the sunset over the river. You don't need reservations or a plan — just show up, find a patch of grass, and relax.


Photo: Wpcpey / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 — source

Day 3: Day Trip to Suwon — Hwaseong Fortress

For your last day, take a day trip to Suwon, a city just south of Seoul that's directly connected by Subway Line 1 — no KTX or reserved ticket needed, just tap your T-money card like any other subway ride (around 50–60 minutes from central Seoul). Suwon's main attraction is Hwaseong Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with a 5.7 km wall you can walk almost the entire length of. Built in the 1790s by King Jeongjo, it's one of the best-preserved fortress walls in Korea, with gates, pavilions, and watchtowers along the way.

The fortress and the old town around it, Haenggung-dong, were filming locations for the 2024 hit drama Lovely Runner, which brought a wave of fans here on their own mini pilgrimage. Walking the wall takes 2–3 hours at an easy pace; you can also ride the fortress train or a bike-tram partway if you'd rather not walk it all. Before you head back, it's worth stopping at Suwon Starfield Library inside a nearby shopping mall — a free-to-enter, multi-story wall of bookshelves that's become one of the most photographed indoor spots in the Seoul area, drama filming or not.


Photo: Bernard Gagnon / Wikimedia Commons, CC0 — source

One last practical note: active filming sets are almost never open to the public, and production schedules are kept secret, so don't expect to see actors filming live. What you're visiting are the real, already-aired locations — which is exactly what most fans actually want anyway. If you want to chase newer dramas, search "[drama name] + filming location" closer to your trip date, since new spots get discovered within days of an episode airing.

💬 Spotted a filming location we didn't mention, or planning a K-drama trip of your own? Tell us in the comments — we'd love to hear which drama brought you to Korea!
meta_description: A first-timer's 2N3D Seoul K-drama tour: real filming spots like DDP, Namsan, Seongsu cafes, and Suwon's Hwaseong Fortress.
